The circadian clock in mammals temporally coordinates physiological and behavioural processes to anticipate daily rhythmic changes in their environment. Chronic disruption to circadian rhythms (e.g., through ageing or shift work) is thought to contribute to a multitude of diseases, including degeneration of the musculoskeletal system. The intervertebral disc (IVD) in the spine contains circadian clocks which control ∼6% of the transcriptome in a rhythmic manner, including key genes involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis. Consistent with an up-regulation of FOXO1 mRNA and protein levels in Bmal1 knockout IVDs, inhibition of FOXO1 in AF cells suppressed their osteogenic differentiation. Collectively, these data highlight the importance of the local molecular clock mechanism in the maintenance of the cell fate and ECM homeostasis of the IVD. [BACKGROUND]: Intervertebral disc (IVD) is a highly rhythmic tissue, which experiences a diurnal cycle of high/low mechanical loading via the changes of activity/rest phase. [METHODS AND RESULTS]: In this study, we used IL-1β, a commonly used inflammatory factor, to induce IDD and found that the IVD clock was dampened in degenerated human nucleus pulposus specimens, rat nucleus pulposus (NP) tissues, and cells. In addition, NRF2 activation attenuated the dysfunction of NP cells induced by the dampened IVD clock and the degenerative process of NP tissues in an organotypic tissue-explant model.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Taken together, our study extends the relationship between peripheral clock and IVD homeostasis and provides a potential therapeutic method for the prevention and recovery of IDD by targeting the clock-controlled gene Nrf2.

key_findings.finding: Primary evidence establishes an intrinsic peripheral circadian clock in the intervertebral disc: PER2::LUC mouse disc explants showed sustained ~24-hour bioluminescence rhythms (period 23.93±0.10 h) for >5 days, with rhythmic signals in both annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus; human disc cells carrying a Per2::luc reporter also oscillated. The study identified 607 rhythmic IVD transcripts, supporting functional tissue-level clock control. PMID 27489225 (2017).

source_tools.relevance: Primary mouse explant and human disc-cell study; methods and results/abstract

key_findings.finding: The disc clock is age- and cytokine-sensitive: in the 2017 primary study, circadian amplitude was dampened with mouse aging and was abolished by IL-1β treatment, whereas TNF-α did not abolish the rhythm under the tested conditions. Thus, direct evidence is strong for IL-1β-mediated clock disruption but does not support an equivalent effect of TNF-α in that experiment. PMID 27489225.

source_tools.relevance: Direct cytokine and aging comparison in disc explants/cells

key_findings.finding: Disrupting the core clock promotes degeneration: conditional, disc-cell-specific Bmal1 deletion caused age-related IVD degeneration in mice in the 2017 study. A later Col2a1-Bmal1 knockout study found age-related annulus fibrosus ECM microarchitectural changes, an endochondral-ossification-like phenotype, loss of circadian transcript patterns, loss of AF markers, and dysregulated ECM/FOXO pathways, indicating that BMAL1 is required for disc cell fate and matrix homeostasis. key_findings.finding: Degenerated and aged nucleus pulposus cells/tissues have dampened clocks and reduced core clock proteins: in human degenerated NP tissue and rat models, BMAL1 and CLOCK immunoreactivity/expression decreased with degeneration. Excessive mechanical strain inhibited core clock proteins, disrupted rhythms via Rho/ROCK signaling, suppressed ECM genes, and BMAL1 overexpression partly rescued the mechanical-load effect on ECM genes. Long-term circadian disruption and/or loading accelerated rat IDD. PMID 34934193 (2021).

NRF2 activation attenuated NP-cell dysfunction and degeneration in an organotypic explant model. PMID 35922862 (2022).
